# 0. What this document is

This is the same question as before — **which musical attributes predict how long a
track gets listened to?** — asked of the same data, but with the data-quality
problems of the first version fixed and every claim re-derived from scratch.

The first version (preserved, unchanged, in `../work/v1/`, alongside this
repository) concluded that the three
continuous attributes (danceability, energy, tempo) were *"redundant"* given genre
and artist, and that the model *"does not predict playback time out of sample"*.
Neither conclusion holds up as stated. One is reversed here; the other is true only
on the untransformed scale. This version supersedes both, and Section 7 states exactly
what changed.

The short answer this analysis supports:

> **Genre and artist explain a modest share of the variation in listening
> behaviour, and a small amount of the rest is associated with the audio
> attributes — but that association is not one effect. It is a negative association
> with *falling below one full play*, and a weak association with how much a track is
> played once it is already playing; the pooled coefficient is not an average of the
> two, because they are measured on different scales, and what it mostly measures is
> **whether a track is reached at all**. Genre and artist remain much the stronger
> predictors, and the three audio attributes add about a quarter of a percentage
> point on top of them.**

Everything below is computed from the raw CSV in this document; there are no
saved intermediate objects.

```{r libs}
have_nlme <- has("nlme")   # ships with R; used only for the mixed-model check
```

# 1. Data and the unit of observation

The file has `r nrow(read.csv("data/Spotify_Song_Attributes.csv"))` rows and 22
columns. Before anything else: what is a row?

```{r unit}
raw <- read.csv("data/Spotify_Song_Attributes.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
pair <- paste(raw$trackName, raw$artistName)
cat("rows                        :", nrow(raw), "\n")
cat("distinct (track, artist)    :", length(unique(pair)), "\n")
cat("copies per track            :", paste(names(table(table(pair))), table(table(pair)), sep = "x", collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("any timestamp / user / session column:",
    any(tolower(names(raw)) %in% c("ts", "user", "date", "endtime", "played_at")), "\n")
```

Every track appears **exactly twice**, and the two copies are identical in every
column that is not part of the key — not merely similar. The file cannot tell us
which step produced it, but the pattern is what a join on a non-unique key leaves
behind, and two further facts point the same way.

```{r dup-mechanism}
same <- sapply(split(seq_len(nrow(raw)), pair),
               function(i) all(sapply(raw[i, -1], function(v) length(unique(v)) == 1)))
id_count <- table(raw$id[raw$id != ""])
cat("identical within pair, non-key columns :", all(same), "\n")
cat("ids shared by two DIFFERENT titles    :",
    sum(sapply(names(id_count[id_count == 4]), function(i) length(unique(raw$trackName[raw$id == i])) == 2)), "\n")
cat("rows with a blank id (failed join)    :", sum(raw$id == ""), "\n")
```

The 29 ids that appear four times are each shared by **two different titles**
(usually a track and another version of the same song). That is the signature of a
join on `id` rather than on `id` plus a title key — and it has a consequence the
first version never drew: those 58 tracks were given audio features looked up under
an id that also belongs to another recording, so some of their features may describe
the other version. The 550 blank-id rows carry no audio features at all, which is
what the unmatched arm of such a join looks like: their metadata came through, their
audio lookup did not.

**The unit of observation is one track, not one row.** All analysis below uses
`r length(unique(pair))` distinct tracks. Nothing about the coefficients of an
ordinary least-squares fit changes when you duplicate rows, which is why the
first version's estimates looked plausible. The first version did notice the
duplication and said so in its closing section, but its models were fitted before
that point and were never re-fitted; the effect is that everything about its *inference*
changes, because standard errors, p-values, AIC and every count were computed on
twice as much data as existed.

```{r dedupe}
d <- raw[!duplicated(pair), ]
stopifnot(nrow(d) == length(unique(pair)))
d$artist_full <- trimws(d$artistName)   # kept uncut, for the dependence check in 5.3
```

## 1.1 What the response actually measures

`msPlayed` is cumulative time, not the length of one play. Comparing it to the
track's own duration (which the file provides) tells us whether a track was
skipped, played once, or repeated.

```{r response}
audio_vars <- c("danceability", "energy", "key", "loudness", "mode", "speechiness",
                "acousticness", "instrumentalness", "liveness", "valence", "tempo",
                "duration_ms", "time_signature")
d$audio_missing <- apply(d[, audio_vars], 1, function(r) all(is.na(r) | r == ""))
d$plays <- d$msPlayed / d$duration_ms

skip_share <- mean(d$plays < 1, na.rm = TRUE)
cat("tracks with no audio features at all :", sum(d$audio_missing), "\n")
cat("share of tracks below one full play  :", sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * skip_share), "\n")
cat("share below half a play              :", sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * mean(d$plays < 0.5, na.rm = TRUE)), "\n")
cat("median plays (tracks that were started):", sprintf("%.2f", median(d$plays, na.rm = TRUE)), "\n")
cat("maximum plays                        :", sprintf("%.0f", max(d$plays, na.rm = TRUE)), "\n")
cat("maximum msPlayed                     :", sprintf("%.1f hours", max(d$msPlayed)/3.6e6), "\n")
```

`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * skip_share)` of tracks were abandoned before one full
play's worth of listening accumulated, while a few were repeated hundreds of
times. `msPlayed` is therefore a *mixture* of two behaviours — the decision to
skip and the amount of listening given a non-skip — and a single linear model on
the raw total answers neither question precisely. This is the central structural
fact about the data, and Section 6 takes it seriously.

## 1.2 Missingness

```{r missing}
d$genre_missing <- is.na(d$genre) | trimws(d$genre) == ""
cat("genre missing            :", sum(d$genre_missing), sprintf("(%.1f%%)", 100 * mean(d$genre_missing)), "\n")
cat("all audio missing        :", sum(d$audio_missing), sprintf("(%.1f%%)", 100 * mean(d$audio_missing)), "\n")
cat("  of which genre missing :", sum(d$audio_missing & d$genre_missing), "\n")
cat("median msPlayed, audio present :", sprintf("%.0f", median(d$msPlayed[!d$audio_missing])), "\n")
cat("median msPlayed, audio missing :", sprintf("%.0f", median(d$msPlayed[d$audio_missing])), "\n")
```

The two missingness patterns are different problems and deserve different
treatments: a missing **genre** is a missing label on an otherwise measured
track, while missing **audio** is a track that never matched the audio-features
source at all. The first version imputed the audio columns for those tracks with
k-nearest neighbours. That is not defensible here:

* the neighbour metric was computed over all 22 columns, which includes
  `msPlayed` — the response variable — so the imputed covariates were partly a
  function of the outcome;
* the result was degenerate: the imputed rows collapsed onto essentially one
  donor value (imputed energy had *zero* variance), so 550 rows were assigned a
  fabricated point mass rather than a plausible measurement;
* the 275 affected tracks are not a random sample — they have a lower median
  playback and no genre at all.

Those 275 tracks are therefore **excluded from the models that use audio
features** and retained (with an explicit indicator) in a sensitivity model in
Section 5.4. That is a real limitation, stated as such, rather than papered over
with imputed numbers.

# 2. Preprocessing

The cleaning logic is the first version's, with the defects corrected. What
changed, and why:

| v1 choice | v2 choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Modelled 10,080 rows | 5,040 distinct tracks | Rows were an exact 2x duplication (Section 1) |
| kNN imputation over all 22 columns | No imputation; 275 no-audio tracks excluded from audio models, with an indicator sensitivity model | Response leaked into the neighbour metric; imputation was degenerate |
| Rare-genre filter applied before the genre mapping | Applied after the mapping | In v1 the filter compared mapped labels against counts of *raw* labels, so it silently matched nothing and levels meant to be collapsed survived |
| Missing genre to `"Other"` | Missing genre to its own `"Unspecified"` level | `"Other"` already means "rare label"; conflating it with "not recorded" mixes two different things (29% of v1's `Other` was actually missing data) |
| Artist: collapse empty names to `"Other"`, then `tolower()` | Transliterate from UTF-8, lowercase first, then collapse | In v1 the ordering produced two distinct levels, `"Other"` and `"other"` (6,164 vs 44 tracks), the smaller being an artefact of stripping accents and non-Latin characters |
| Rare-artist threshold `< 10` applied to duplicated counts | Applied to distinct tracks | Duplication doubled every count, so the threshold kept many artists that only qualified because their rows were counted twice (178 levels to 52) |
| IQR capping and min-max scaling of predictors | Untouched raw units; standardised effects reported instead | Capping moved 178 legitimately low-danceability tracks and clipped 24 tempo values; min-max is a linear rescale that changes no R² and destroys interpretability |
| Reference levels set implicitly by alphabetical order | Set explicitly to the most frequent level | Alphabetical reference levels are an accident of spelling, and here they happened to be tiny categories |
| Response untransformed (skew 13.6) | log10(msPlayed + 1) | See Section 2.1 |

```{r prep-genre}
d$genre <- ifelse(d$genre_missing, NA, tolower(d$genre))
genre_mapping <- c(
  "alt z" = "alternative", "album rock" = "rock", "british orchestra" = "classical",
  "desi hip hop" = "hip hop", "bedroom r&b" = "r&b", "singer-songwriter pop" = "pop",
  "la pop" = "pop", "lo-fi chill" = "lo-fi", "orchestral soundtrack" = "classical",
  "comic" = "other", "alternative metal" = "metal", "deep underground hip hop" = "hip hop",
  "pop" = "pop", "classical" = "classical", "modern alternative rock" = "alternative",
  "scandipop" = "pop", "punjabi pop" = "pop", "folk-pop" = "folk", "acoustic pop" = "pop",
  "art pop" = "pop", "electronica" = "electronic", "dance pop" = "pop",
  "bedroom pop" = "pop", "chill r&b" = "r&b", "indian lo-fi" = "lo-fi",
  "instrumental post-rock" = "post-rock", "classic bollywood" = "bollywood",
  "afghan pop" = "pop", "classic rock" = "rock", "german soundtrack" = "classical",
  "anime lo-fi" = "lo-fi", "lo-fi study" = "lo-fi", "dark r&b" = "r&b",
  "modern indie pop" = "indie", "pop edm" = "edm", "uk contemporary r&b" = "r&b",
  "emo rap" = "hip hop", "classic pakistani pop" = "pop", "japanese chillhop" = "chillhop",
  "japanese vgm" = "vgm", "anime" = "other", "bhangra" = "indian",
  "afrobeats" = "afrobeat", "j-pop" = "asian pop", "k-pop" = "asian pop")
hit <- !is.na(d$genre) & d$genre %in% names(genre_mapping)
d$genre[hit] <- genre_mapping[d$genre[hit]]
d$genre[!is.na(d$genre) & d$genre == "other"] <- "Other"
d$genre[is.na(d$genre)] <- "Unspecified"

# rare-genre collapse, applied AFTER the mapping (the v1 filter ran on stale counts)
gc50 <- table(d$genre)
rare <- names(gc50[gc50 < 50 & names(gc50) != "Unspecified"])
d$genre <- ifelse(d$genre %in% rare, "Other", d$genre)
```

```{r prep-artist}
a <- trimws(d$artistName)
a_tr <- iconv(a, from = "UTF-8", to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT")   # keep accents as letters
a_tr[is.na(a_tr)] <- a[is.na(a_tr)]
a <- a_tr
subs <- data.frame(
  pat = c("\\$", "@", "&", "!", "#", "\\*", "%", "\\.", ",", "\\(", "\\)", "\\[", "\\]"),
  rep = c("s", "a", " and ", "", "", "", " percent ", "", "", "", "", "", ""),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(subs))) a <- gsub(subs$pat[i], subs$rep[i], a)
a <- tolower(gsub("\\s+", " ", trimws(gsub("[^a-zA-Z0-9 ]", "", a))))
a[nchar(a) == 0] <- "other"
ac <- table(a)
a[a %in% names(ac[ac < 10 & names(ac) != "other"])] <- "Other"
a[a == "other"] <- "Other"          # names that did not survive at all are not identities
d$artistName <- a
```

```{r prep-final}
d$log_msPlayed <- log10(d$msPlayed + 1)
ref_genre  <- names(sort(table(d$genre), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
ref_artist <- names(sort(table(d$artistName), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
d$genre      <- relevel(factor(d$genre), ref = ref_genre)
d$artistName <- relevel(factor(d$artistName), ref = ref_artist)

ca <- d[!d$audio_missing, ]          # complete-audio tracks: the modelling sample
ca$genre <- droplevels(ca$genre); ca$artistName <- droplevels(ca$artistName)
cat("distinct tracks                  :", nrow(d), "\n")
cat("with complete audio features     :", nrow(ca), "\n")
cat("genre levels                     :", nlevels(ca$genre), "\n")
cat("artist levels                    :", nlevels(ca$artistName), "\n")
cat("reference level            : genre =", levels(ca$genre)[1],
    "| artist =", levels(ca$artistName)[1], "\n")
cat("\ngenre distribution in the modelling sample:\n")
print(sort(table(ca$genre), decreasing = TRUE))
```

## 2.1 The response transformation

```{r transform}
skew <- function(x) { x <- x - mean(x); mean(x^3) / mean(x^2)^1.5 }
kur  <- function(x) { x <- x - mean(x); mean(x^4) / mean(x^2)^2 - 3 }
prof <- function(lam) {
  y  <- if (abs(lam) < 1e-9) log(d$msPlayed + 1) else ((d$msPlayed + 1)^lam - 1) / lam
  m  <- lm(y ~ 1); n <- length(y)
  -n/2 * (log(2 * pi) + log(sum(resid(m)^2) / n) + 1) + (lam - 1) * sum(log(d$msPlayed + 1))
}
lams <- seq(-0.4, 0.5, 0.005); ll <- sapply(lams, prof)
lam_hat <- lams[which.max(ll)]
cat("skewness, raw msPlayed :", sprintf("%.2f", skew(d$msPlayed)), "\n")
cat("skewness, log10(ms+1)  :", sprintf("%.2f", skew(d$log_msPlayed)), "\n")
cat("Box-Cox MLE lambda     :", sprintf("%.3f", lam_hat), "\n")
cat("LR both ways vs lambda = 0 :", sprintf("%.1f", 2 * (max(ll) - prof(0))), "\n")
```

A log transform is conventional for a response like this, but the profile
likelihood prefers a mild positive power, and $\lambda = 0$ is rejected. The
practical difference is small and both scales are carried through the
specification curve in Section 5.2; `log10(msPlayed + 1)` is the primary scale
because it is standard, interpretable as a proportional change, and — as Section
1.1 showed — it is the scale on which the skip/repeat mixture shows up as a
distributional feature rather than as a handful of impossible outliers.

# 3. Exploratory analysis

```{r eda-response, fig.cap="Response on three scales. The raw scale hides its own tail: the mass sits in the first bin and the 40-hour tracks are invisible. On the log scale the skip/non-skip split appears as a separate left mode, and `plays` shows it directly."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
hist(d$msPlayed / 60000, breaks = 60, col = "grey80", border = "white",
     main = "raw (minutes)", xlab = "minutes", xlim = c(0, 300))
hist(d$log_msPlayed, breaks = 40, col = "grey80", border = "white",
     main = "log10(msPlayed + 1)", xlab = "log10(msPlayed + 1)")
hist(log10(d$plays), breaks = 40, col = "grey80", border = "white",
     main = "plays = msPlayed / duration", xlab = "log10(plays)", xlim = c(-3, 4))
abline(v = 0, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
```

```{r eda-cor}
cvars <- c("danceability", "energy", "tempo")
cat("correlation with log10(msPlayed + 1):\n")
print(round(rbind(Pearson  = sapply(cvars, function(v) cor(ca[[v]], ca$log_msPlayed)),
                  Spearman = sapply(cvars, function(v)
                    cor(ca[[v]], ca$log_msPlayed, method = "spearman"))), 3))
cat("\ncorrelation among the attributes:\n")
print(round(cor(ca[, cvars]), 3))
```

Two near-zero correlations with the outcome, and weak collinearity among the
attributes themselves. Neither fact settles whether the attributes are redundant:
redundancy is a question about what a model gains, not about pairwise correlations
(Section 4 answers it that way). What the correlations do rule out is the reading
that these three variables are a re-encoding of genre — they are largely separate
information (Section 7 quantifies how much genre and artist actually recover).

```{r eda-genre, fig.cap="Listening by genre. Differences between genre medians are visible but modest; the spread within any genre dwarfs them."}
boxplot(ca$log_msPlayed ~ ca$genre, las = 2, col = "grey85", border = "grey40",
        ylab = "log10(msPlayed + 1)", xlab = "genre", cex.axis = .7, outline = FALSE)
```

```{r eda-skip}
cat("share of tracks skipped before one full play, by genre:\n")
print(round(sort(tapply(ca$plays < 1, ca$genre, mean), decreasing = TRUE), 3))
```

# 4. Do the attributes add anything beyond genre and artist?

The model ladder answers exactly one question: **given genre and artist, do
danceability, energy and tempo carry additional information about listening?**
Everything is on the log scale, on distinct tracks, with audio features present.

```{r ladder}
f <- list(
  M0 = log_msPlayed ~ 1,
  M1 = log_msPlayed ~ danceability + energy + tempo,
  M2 = log_msPlayed ~ genre,
  M3 = log_msPlayed ~ artistName,
  M4 = log_msPlayed ~ genre + artistName,
  M5 = log_msPlayed ~ danceability + energy + tempo + genre + artistName,
  M6 = log_msPlayed ~ (danceability + energy + tempo) * genre + artistName)
fit <- lapply(f, function(fm) lm(fm, data = ca))
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fit), function(nm) {
  m <- fit[[nm]]
  data.frame(model = nm, params = length(coef(m)),
             R2 = summary(m)$r.squared, adjR2 = summary(m)$adj.r.squared,
             AIC = AIC(m), BIC = BIC(m))
}))
print(tab, row.names = FALSE, digits = 4)
```

```{r blocks}
r2 <- function(m) summary(m)$r.squared
tests <- list(c("M0","M1"), c("M0","M2"), c("M0","M3"), c("M4","M5"),
              c("M5","M6"), c("M2","M4"), c("M3","M4"))
lab <- c("audio alone", "genre alone", "artist alone", "audio | genre+artist",
         "interactions | main effects", "artist | genre", "genre | artist")
bt <- data.frame(comparison = lab,
                 dR2 = c(r2(fit$M1) - r2(fit$M0), r2(fit$M2) - r2(fit$M0),
                         r2(fit$M3) - r2(fit$M0), r2(fit$M5) - r2(fit$M4),
                         r2(fit$M6) - r2(fit$M5), r2(fit$M4) - r2(fit$M2),
                         r2(fit$M4) - r2(fit$M3)))
for (i in seq_along(tests)) {
  a <- anova(fit[[tests[[i]][1]]], fit[[tests[[i]][2]]])
  bt$num_df[i] <- a$Df[2]; bt$den_df[i] <- a$Res.Df[2]
  bt$F[i] <- a$F[2]; bt$p[i] <- a$`Pr(>F)`[2]
}
bt$dR2 <- round(bt$dR2, 4); bt$F <- round(bt$F, 3); bt$p <- signif(bt$p, 3)
print(bt, row.names = FALSE)
```

Three things to read off this table.

1. **Genre and artist both matter, and neither is redundant to the other** by these
   tests — though BIC, with its heavier penalty, is willing to spend the artist
   parameters and keep only genre. Each
   adds significantly over the other (artist given genre
   p = `r sprintf("%.2g", bt$p[6])`; genre given artist
   p = `r sprintf("%.2g", bt$p[7])`). Together they explain
   `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * r2(fit$M4))` of the log-variance.
2. **The audio attributes add a small but detectable increment** —
   $\Delta R^2 = `r sprintf("%.4f", r2(fit$M5) - r2(fit$M4))`$,
   `r sprintf("F(%d, %d) = %.2f", bt$num_df[4], bt$den_df[4], bt$F[4])`, p =
   `r sprintf("%.4f", bt$p[4])`.
   That is about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (r2(fit$M5) - r2(fit$M4)) / r2(fit$M5))` of
   the model's explained variance — small, but not zero.
3. **Interactions are not supported.** 39 extra parameters buy
   `r sprintf("%.4f", r2(fit$M6) - r2(fit$M5))` of R² and fail
   (p = `r sprintf("%.2f", bt$p[5])`); both AIC and BIC penalise the model.

The information criteria do not agree with each other, and that disagreement is part
of the honest summary: AIC prefers M5, but **BIC prefers M2 — genre alone**, which
drops both the audio block and the 51 artist parameters. BIC is telling us these data
do not fund a 68-parameter model, and that is a fair reading; nothing later in this
document resolves it. Section 5.2 shows which parts of the result depend on the
analyst's choices and which do not.

## 4.1 Which attribute?

```{r coefs}
m5 <- fit$M5
X  <- model.matrix(m5); e <- resid(m5); h <- hatvalues(m5)
bread <- solve(crossprod(X))
V_hc3 <- bread %*% crossprod(X * (e / (1 - h))^2, X) %*% bread
V_cl  <- vcov(m5)
out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("danceability", "energy", "tempo"), function(v) {
  b <- coef(m5)[v]; se <- sqrt(V_hc3[v, v]); s <- sd(ca[[v]])
  data.frame(attribute = v, b = b, SE_OLS = sqrt(V_cl[v, v]), SE_HC3 = se,
             t = b / se, p = 2 * pt(-abs(b / se), df.residual(m5)),
             pct_per_SD = (10^(b * s) - 1) * 100)
}))
out[, 2:7] <- round(out[, 2:7], 4)
print(out, row.names = FALSE)
```

Only **energy** is distinguishable from zero once genre and artist are held
fixed, and its sign is negative: a one-standard-deviation increase in energy is
associated with about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", abs(out$pct_per_SD[2]))` *less*
listening time on the log scale. Danceability and tempo are not estimated
precisely enough to support any direction. Section 6 takes this coefficient apart:
it is the sum of a negative association with skipping and a positive association with
duration, not a duration effect on its own.

## 4.2 Diagnostics

```{r diag}
res <- resid(m5)
aux <- summary(lm(I(res^2) ~ fitted(m5)))
bp  <- aux$r.squared * length(res)
cat("Breusch-Pagan (n x R2 of auxiliary regression) :",
    sprintf("%.1f, p = %.4g", bp, pchisq(bp, 1, lower.tail = FALSE)), "\n")
cat("residual skew / excess kurtosis                :",
    sprintf("%.2f / %.2f", skew(res), kur(res)), "\n")
cat("Shapiro-Wilk (2000-residual sample)            :",
    sprintf("W = %.3f", shapiro.test(sample(res, 2000))$statistic), "\n")
cd <- cooks.distance(m5)
cat("Cook's D > 4/n                                 :", sum(cd > 4 / nrow(ca)),
    sprintf("(%.1f%%), max %.3f", 100 * mean(cd > 4 / nrow(ca)), max(cd)), "\n")
Xf <- X[, -1]
vif <- sapply(c("danceability", "energy", "tempo"), function(v)
  1 / (1 - summary(lm(Xf[, v] ~ Xf[, setdiff(colnames(Xf), v)]))$r.squared))
cat("VIF against the full design                    :", round(vif, 2), "\n")
cat("condition number (continuous scaled)           :",
    round(kappa(cbind(scale(Xf[, 1:3]), Xf[, -(1:4)])), 1), "\n")
# the same diagnostics on the RAW scale, so the comparison in 5.2 is an observed one
raw5 <- lm(msPlayed ~ danceability + energy + tempo + genre + artistName, data = ca)
bres <- summary(lm(I(resid(raw5)^2) ~ fitted(raw5)))$r.squared * nrow(ca)
cat("raw scale: Breusch-Pagan p =", signif(pchisq(bres, 1, lower.tail = FALSE), 3),
    "| residual skew =", sprintf("%.1f", skew(resid(raw5))), "\n")
```

```{r diag-plots, fig.cap="Residual diagnostics. The mild funnel in the scale-location plot is why robust standard errors are reported; the Q-Q deviation reflects the skip/repeat mixture rather than a few influential points."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(fitted(m5), res, pch = 20, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, .25), cex = .6,
     xlab = "fitted", ylab = "residual", main = "residuals vs fitted")
abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick")
plot(fitted(m5), sqrt(abs(scale(res))), pch = 20, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, .25), cex = .6,
     xlab = "fitted", ylab = "sqrt|std resid|", main = "scale-location")
qqnorm(rstandard(m5), pch = 20, cex = .5, main = "Q-Q (normal)")
qqline(rstandard(m5), col = "firebrick")
```

Heteroscedasticity is present and modest, residuals are far from normal, and no
observation is influential (largest Cook's D
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(cd))`, far below 1). The non-normality is a *shape*
problem — the response is a crossing of two behaviours — not an outlier problem,
which is why the remedy is to report HC3 standard errors and to decompose the
response (Section 6) rather than to delete points.

# 5. Out of sample, robustly

## 5.1 One split is an anecdote

The first version reported a single 70/30 split. A 1,400-track test set has an R²
standard error of roughly 0.02, which is eight to twenty times the increment under
discussion — so one split cannot settle anything. Repeating it 200 times says what
the model actually delivers.

```{r cv}
set.seed(7); B <- 200
mtx <- sapply(names(f), function(nm) numeric(B))
for (b in 1:B) {
  tr <- sample(nrow(ca), floor(.7 * nrow(ca)))
  for (nm in names(f)) {
    m <- lm(f[[nm]], ca[tr, ]); p <- predict(m, ca[-tr, ])
    ok <- !is.na(p); yt <- ca$log_msPlayed[-tr][ok]
    mtx[, nm][b] <- 1 - sum((yt - p[ok])^2) / sum((yt - mean(ca$log_msPlayed[tr]))^2)
  }
}
cvtab <- data.frame(model = colnames(mtx), test_R2 = colMeans(mtx),
                    sd = apply(mtx, 2, sd),
                    lo = apply(mtx, 2, quantile, .025),
                    hi = apply(mtx, 2, quantile, .975))
cvtab[, 2:5] <- round(cvtab[, 2:5], 4)
print(cvtab, row.names = FALSE)
dlt <- mtx[, "M5"] - mtx[, "M4"]
cat("\naudio increment out of sample: mean", sprintf("%+.4f", mean(dlt)),
    "95% [", sprintf("%+.4f", quantile(dlt, .025)), ",",
    sprintf("%+.4f", quantile(dlt, .975)), "] positive in",
    sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(dlt > 0)), "of splits\n")

# the same model on the raw scale, which is the series the first version reported
raw_r2 <- numeric(B); set.seed(7)
for (b in 1:B) {
  tr <- sample(nrow(ca), floor(.7 * nrow(ca)))
  m  <- lm(msPlayed ~ danceability + energy + tempo + genre + artistName, ca[tr, ])
  pr <- predict(m, ca[-tr, ]); yt <- ca$msPlayed[-tr]
  raw_r2[b] <- 1 - sum((yt - pr)^2) / sum((yt - mean(ca$msPlayed[tr]))^2)
}
cat("same wide model, raw msPlayed scale: mean test R2 =",
    sprintf("%.3f", mean(raw_r2)), "| negative in",
    sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(raw_r2 < 0)), "of splits\n")
```

One of these overturns the first version's conclusion; the other agrees with its
caution, but for a completely different reason.

* **The model does generalise.** In at least 97.5% of splits every categorical model
  has a positive test R² (the 2.5% quantile is above zero for all of them), and the
  wide model averages `r sprintf("%.3f", round(mean(mtx[, "M5"]), 3))`. The earlier
  claim that the model "does not predict playback time out of sample" was a
  property of the *raw response scale*, not of the model: the identical specification
  on `msPlayed` in milliseconds averages
  `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(raw_r2))` across the same 200 splits, and is negative in
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(raw_r2 < 0))` of them, because a handful of
  enormous values dominate squared error. On a variance-stabilised scale the same
  model is modest but genuinely predictive.
* **The audio increment does not clearly survive out of sample**: mean
  `r sprintf("%+.4f", mean(dlt))`, interval
  `r sprintf("[%+.4f, %+.4f]", quantile(dlt, .025), quantile(dlt, .975))`, positive in
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(dlt > 0))` of splits. In-sample detectability and
  out-of-sample usefulness are different claims, and the attributes have more of
  the first than the second.

## 5.2 Does the conclusion depend on my choices?

A p-value from one specification is worth little if defensible alternatives
disagree. The grid below crosses the response scale (log, Box-Cox, raw) with two
genre codings and two artist codings and re-tests the audio block in each.

```{r spec-curve}
g_as_is <- as.character(ca$genre)
g_other <- { g <- g_as_is; g[g == "Unspecified"] <- "Other"; g }
gv <- list(as_is = g_as_is, unspecified_as_other = g_other)
spec <- data.frame()
for (tn in c("log10", "boxcox", "raw")) {
  yy <- switch(tn,
    log10  = log10(ca$msPlayed + 1),
    boxcox = ((ca$msPlayed + 1)^lam_hat - 1) / lam_hat,
    raw    = ca$msPlayed)
  for (gn in names(gv)) for (ar in c("52-level", "named vs Other")) {
    art <- if (ar == "52-level") factor(ca$artistName)
           else factor(ifelse(as.character(ca$artistName) == "Other", "Other", "named"),
                       levels = c("Other", "named"))
    dd <- data.frame(y = yy, danceability = ca$danceability, energy = ca$energy,
                     tempo = ca$tempo, genre = factor(gv[[gn]]), artist = art)
    r0 <- lm(y ~ genre + artist, dd)
    r1 <- lm(y ~ danceability + energy + tempo + genre + artist, dd)
    spec <- rbind(spec, data.frame(scale = tn, genre = gn, artist = ar,
                                   p = anova(r0, r1)$`Pr(>F)`[2]))
  }
}
spec <- spec[order(spec$p), ]
print(spec, row.names = FALSE, digits = 3)
cat("\nrange of the audio-block p-value:", sprintf("%.4f", min(spec$p)), "to",
    sprintf("%.4f", max(spec$p)), "|", sum(spec$p < .05), "of", nrow(spec),
    "specifications below 0.05\n")
```

Read this table narrowly. The audio block clears 0.05 under the two near-log
transforms and under neither raw-scale variant. Within a given scale, changing the
genre or artist *coding* moves p by less than 0.002, so the result is not an artefact
of how the dummies were built — but *between* scales the same recoding moves it a
great deal (0.49 to 0.14 on the raw scale), which is exactly the point: scale
dominates coding. The two power transforms are also close enough to each other
(λ = 0 and λ = 0.110) that they are barely two independent specifications. What the table shows is that the
result is not an artefact of how the dummies were built; it does not show that the
effect is robust to every choice, and the raw-scale p-values (0.14–0.49) are
uncontrolled by any robust inference, so they are not evidence against the effect
either.

The choice that moves the headline R² most is **artist pruning**, which the grid
above does not touch. The first version kept 178 artist levels; this version keeps
52. Both are defensible, and they are not equivalent.

```{r threshold}
ca$artist_raw <- trimws(d$artist_full[!d$audio_missing])
thr <- data.frame()
for (k in c(10, 25, 50, 0)) {
  a2 <- if (k == 0) factor(ca$artist_raw) else {
    tt <- table(ca$artist_raw); keep <- names(tt[tt >= k])
    factor(ifelse(ca$artist_raw %in% keep, ca$artist_raw, "Other"))
  }
  dd <- data.frame(y = ca$log_msPlayed, danceability = ca$danceability,
                   energy = ca$energy, tempo = ca$tempo,
                   genre = factor(as.character(ca$genre)), artist = a2)
  r0 <- lm(y ~ genre + artist, dd)
  r1 <- lm(y ~ danceability + energy + tempo + genre + artist, dd)
  thr <- rbind(thr, data.frame(
    artists = if (k == 0) "kept all" else paste0(">=", k, " tracks"),
    levels = nlevels(a2), params = length(coef(r1)),
    R2 = summary(r1)$r.squared, p_audio = anova(r0, r1)[["Pr(>F)"]][2]))
}
thr$R2 <- round(thr$R2, 4); thr$p_audio <- signif(thr$p_audio, 3)
print(thr, row.names = FALSE)

# and what the unpruned design costs out of sample (about 8 s per split)
Xa <- model.matrix(~ danceability + energy + tempo + genre + factor(artist_raw),
                   data = ca)
ya <- ca$log_msPlayed
set.seed(5); r2a <- numeric(5)
for (b in 1:5) {
  tr <- sample(nrow(ca), floor(.7 * nrow(ca)))
  cf <- qr.coef(qr(Xa[tr, ]), ya[tr]); cf[is.na(cf)] <- 0
  pr <- as.vector(Xa[-tr, ] %*% cf)
  r2a[b] <- 1 - sum((ya[-tr] - pr)^2) / sum((ya[-tr] - mean(ya[tr]))^2)
}
cat(sprintf("unpruned design, %d splits: mean test R2 %.3f (sd %.3f), negative in %d of %d\n",
            length(r2a), mean(r2a), sd(r2a), sum(r2a < 0), length(r2a)))
```

R² rises steadily with the number of artist levels — from
`r sprintf("%.3f", min(thr$R2))` at the strictest pruning to
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(thr$R2))` when every name is its own dummy — while the
audio block stays significant throughout. That upward drift is why the ceiling in
Section 7 has to be stated as a property of a threshold rather than of the data:
most of the extra R² comes from fitting thousands of artist-specific means to
4,765 tracks, not from new information. Pruning at 10 is the choice this analysis makes, and it is worth being explicit
that it is a choice rather than a discovery: it retains enough artists to say
something about artist identity, it does not collapse the artist axis to essentially
one artist (which is what the >=50 row does), and it is not the row that maximises
R². A reader who wants the higher R² has to buy 2,187 artist dummies for 4,765
tracks, and the last line of output above is what that buys out of sample: the
unpruned design explains 57% of variance in sample and predicts *worse than the
mean* on held-out tracks, in every split tried. The extra R² is memorisation.

## 5.3 Dependence between tracks of the same artist

Artists contribute several tracks each, so their tracks are not independent
observations, and ignoring that understates standard errors.

```{r dep}
if (have_nlme) {
  m_a <- nlme::lme(log_msPlayed ~ genre + danceability + energy + tempo,
                   random = ~ 1 | artist_raw, data = ca, method = "ML")
  m_0 <- nlme::lme(log_msPlayed ~ genre, random = ~ 1 | artist_raw,
                   data = ca, method = "ML")
  v <- nlme::VarCorr(m_a); bs <- as.numeric(v[1, 2]); rs <- as.numeric(v[2, 2])
  icc <- bs^2 / (bs^2 + rs^2)
  cat(sprintf("between-artist SD %.3f | residual SD %.3f | ICC %.3f\n", bs, rs, icc))
  L <- 2 * (as.numeric(logLik(m_a)) - as.numeric(logLik(m_0)))
  cat(sprintf("audio block inside the random-intercept model: LRT chi2 = %.2f on 3 df, p = %.4g\n",
              L, pchisq(L, 3, lower.tail = FALSE)))
} else {
  icc <- NA; cat("nlme not available - dependence check skipped\n")
}

# clustering is a different problem from heteroscedasticity, and needs its own fix
g  <- droplevels(factor(ca$artist_raw))
Xc <- model.matrix(m5); ec <- resid(m5); bm <- solve(crossprod(Xc))
sG <- rowsum(Xc * ec, g)
Vcl <- bm %*% crossprod(sG) %*% bm
idx <- c("danceability", "energy", "tempo"); b3 <- coef(m5)[idx]
Wcl <- as.numeric(t(b3) %*% solve(Vcl[idx, idx]) %*% b3)
cr1 <- (nlevels(g) / (nlevels(g) - 1)) * ((nrow(ca) - 1) / (nrow(ca) - qr(Xc)$rank))
Wcl <- Wcl * cr1
cat(sprintf("artist-clustered Wald for the audio block: chi2 = %.2f on 3 df, p = %.3g (%d clusters)\n",
            Wcl, pchisq(Wcl, 3, lower.tail = FALSE), nlevels(g)))
```

Artist identity accounts for around
`r if (!is.na(icc)) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * icc) else "(see summary)"` of the
residual variance once genre is in the model, and the audio block survives that
reframing as well as the cluster-robust Wald above. The small association is
therefore not an artefact of pseudo-replication.

The two corrections answer different questions and are not substitutes: HC3
(Section 4.1) fixes heteroscedasticity and assumes independent observations, while
the clustered variance assumes nothing about the variance but allows arbitrary
correlation within an artist. Only the second is a valid check on a model whose
rows are tracks by the same artists, and it is the one to trust here.

## 5.4 Selection: what excluding the 275 tracks costs

```{r selection}
sens <- summary(lm(log10(msPlayed + 1) ~ audio_missing + genre + artistName, data = d))
cat("model on all", nrow(d), "tracks with an indicator for missing audio:\n")
cat("  indicator p =", signif(sens$coefficients["audio_missingTRUE", 4], 3),
    "| estimate =", sprintf("%+.3f", sens$coefficients["audio_missingTRUE", 1]),
    sprintf("(%.0f%% less listening)", 100 * (10^sens$coefficients["audio_missingTRUE", 1] - 1)),
    "\n  R2 =", sprintf("%.4f", sens$r.squared), "\n")
cat("  R2 of the same model on the audio-complete sample:",
    sprintf("%.4f", summary(fit$M4)$r.squared), "\n")
```

That is weak evidence (p = 0.041 on one test, nothing else) that the excluded
tracks differ, and the coefficient says in which direction: they were played less.
They are therefore not missing at random with respect to the outcome. The
exclusion is a real selection effect, it biases the audio-complete sample towards
tracks that were listened to, and it is carried into the limitations rather than
denied.

# 6. The decomposition that changes the answer

Everything above treats `msPlayed` as one response. It is two: whether a track was
skipped, and how much it was played if not. Splitting the question this way
resolves the apparent tension of Section 4.1 — that energy is "significant" while
the association is tiny.

```{r hurdle}
ca$skip <- as.integer(ca$plays < 1)
lg0 <- glm(skip ~ genre + artistName, data = ca, family = binomial)
lg1 <- glm(skip ~ danceability + energy + tempo + genre + artistName, data = ca, family = binomial)
cat("=== EXTENSIVE margin: P(skipped before one full play) ===\n")
print(anova(lg0, lg1, test = "LRT"))
bidx <- c("danceability", "energy", "tempo")
Vg <- vcov(lg1); bg <- coef(lg1)[bidx]
W  <- as.numeric(t(bg) %*% solve(Vg[bidx, bidx]) %*% bg)
cat(sprintf("Wald for the audio block: chi2 = %.2f on 3 df, p = %.3g\n",
            W, pchisq(W, 3, lower.tail = FALSE)))
lgt <- summary(lg1)$coefficients[c("danceability", "energy", "tempo"), c(1, 2, 4)]
colnames(lgt) <- c("log_odds", "SE", "p"); lgt <- round(lgt, 4)
cat("\nlogistic coefficients on the skip margin:\n"); print(lgt)
OR <- exp(coef(lg1)["energy"] * sd(ca$energy))
cat(sprintf("energy odds ratio per SD: %.3f\n", OR))
hi <- ca$energy >= quantile(ca$energy, .9)
cat(sprintf("skip rate, top energy decile: %.1f%% | below: %.1f%%\n",
            100 * mean(ca$skip[hi]), 100 * mean(ca$skip[!hi])))

sub <- ca[ca$skip == 0, ]
mi0 <- lm(log_msPlayed ~ genre + artistName, data = sub)
mi1 <- lm(log_msPlayed ~ danceability + energy + tempo + genre + artistName, data = sub)
cat("\n=== INTENSIVE margin: listening given at least one full play (n =", nrow(sub), ") ===\n")
print(anova(mi0, mi1))
p_int <- anova(mi0, mi1)[["Pr(>F)"]][2]
Xi <- model.matrix(mi1); ei <- resid(mi1); hi2 <- hatvalues(mi1)
bi <- solve(crossprod(Xi))
Vi <- bi %*% crossprod(Xi * (ei / (1 - hi2))^2, Xi) %*% bi
se_i <- sqrt(Vi["energy", "energy"])
cat(sprintf("energy, HC3: %+.3f (SE %.3f, p = %.3f)\n", coef(mi1)["energy"], se_i,
            2 * pt(-abs(coef(mi1)["energy"] / se_i), df.residual(mi1))))
cat(sprintf("energy coefficient: %+.3f (p = %.3f)\n", coef(mi1)["energy"],
            summary(mi1)$coefficients["energy", 4]))

# same model on all tracks, with an indicator for having reached one full play
m5s <- lm(log_msPlayed ~ danceability + energy + tempo + skip + genre + artistName,
          data = ca)
cat(sprintf("energy without the skip indicator: %+.4f | with it: %+.4f (p = %.2f)\n",
            coef(m5)["energy"], coef(m5s)["energy"],
            summary(m5s)$coefficients["energy", 4]))
sk <- grep("^skip", names(coef(m5s)), value = TRUE)[1]
ps <- summary(m5s)$coefficients[sk, 4]
cat(sprintf("skip indicator itself (%s): %+.4f (p %s)\n", sk, coef(m5s)[[sk]],
            if (ps < 1e-16) "< 1e-16" else sprintf("= %.2g", ps)))
```

The contrast is stark, and it is the finding:

* On the **extensive** margin the audio block is clearly detected
  (p = `r sprintf("%.1g", pchisq(W, 3, lower.tail = FALSE))`). A
  one-standard-deviation increase in energy multiplies the odds of falling below
  one full play by `r sprintf("%.2f", OR)` — a
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (OR - 1))` increase in the odds. In plain terms,
  tracks in the top energy decile are skipped
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(ca$skip[hi]))` of the time against
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(ca$skip[!hi]))` below it.
* On the **intensive** margin — among tracks played at least once — the *block* is
  not significant (p = `r sprintf("%.2f", p_int)`), but energy taken on its own is —
  at least marginally — and the sign is **reversed**: `r sprintf("%+.3f", coef(mi1)["energy"])`
  (HC3 p = `r sprintf("%.3f", 2 * pt(-abs(coef(mi1)["energy"] / se_i), df.residual(mi1)))`).
  Among tracks that were played, higher energy goes with *more* listening.

The pooled `r sprintf("%+.2f", coef(m5)["energy"])` in Section 4.1 is therefore
**not a weighted average of those two slopes**, and it is worth saying so because the
arithmetic invites it: the skip margin is a log-odds and the duration margin is a
log-time, and `r sprintf("%+.2f", coef(m5)["energy"])` lies outside the interval
spanned by `r sprintf("%+.2f", coef(m5s)["energy"])` and
`r sprintf("%+.3f", coef(mi1)["energy"])`. The decomposition buys direction and
attribution rather than arithmetic: when the model is told whether a track reached
one full play, energy's coefficient moves to
`r sprintf("%+.3f", coef(m5s)["energy"])` (p = `r sprintf("%.2f", summary(m5s)$coefficients["energy", 4])`,
indistinguishable from zero) and the indicator absorbs the association
(`r sprintf("%+.2f", coef(m5s)[[sk]])`).

The two conditional estimates disagree — `r sprintf("%+.3f", coef(mi1)["energy"])`
on the played-only subsample, `r sprintf("%+.3f", coef(m5s)["energy"])` when the
whole sample is modelled with the indicator — but they agree on the thing that
matters: **neither is negative**. What is robustly negative is the association with
reaching a full play at all.

Read this as a measurement problem, not a causal one. The response is cumulative
listening, so "very short" is bounded below by zero while "long" is bounded by
taste, and the same attribute can move the two margins in opposite directions
without contradiction. What the data supports is that energy predicts *abandonment
before one full play*; it does not support a claim about how long a track is enjoyed
once it is being enjoyed.

# 7. What the evidence supports

**On the original question.** Genre and artist are the substantive predictors:
together they explain about `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * r2(fit$M4))` of the variance
in log playback time. The three audio attributes add
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * (r2(fit$M5) - r2(fit$M4)))` percentage points on top of
that, and the increment is statistically detectable
(F = `r sprintf("%.2f", bt$F[4])`, p = `r sprintf("%.4f", bt$p[4])`). Energy's coefficient survives
an HC3 standard error, and the block survives an artist-clustered Wald (p = `r sprintf("%.3g", pchisq(Wcl, 3, lower.tail = FALSE))`) and a
random intercept for artist. It is **not** equally robust elsewhere: it does not
clearly improve out-of-sample prediction
(`r sprintf("%+.4f", mean(dlt))` mean test R², positive in
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(dlt > 0))` of splits), and BIC prefers the model
without it — indeed BIC prefers genre alone over any model that includes the
artist fixed effects.

Of the three attributes, only **energy** is individually distinguishable, and its
single coefficient is the least interesting thing about it: it is negative pooled
(`r sprintf("%+.2f", coef(m5)["energy"])`), negative and strong on the skip margin
(odds ratio `r sprintf("%.2f", OR)` per SD), and positive on the duration margin
(`r sprintf("%+.2f", coef(mi1)["energy"])`, HC3 p = `r sprintf("%.3f", 2 * pt(-abs(coef(mi1)["energy"] / se_i), df.residual(mi1)))`
— marginal, and reported as marginal).
Which of those you call "the effect of energy" is a decision about which question
you are asking, not a fact about the data.

**On the two claims this work supersedes.**

* *"The attributes are redundant given genre and artist."* This is **right about
  the practical consequence and wrong about the reason**. Taking redundancy to mean
  what it has to mean operationally — that the attributes add nothing to a model of
  the outcome — they add
  `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * (r2(fit$M5) - r2(fit$M4)))` percentage points, about
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * (r2(fit$M5) - r2(fit$M4)) / r2(fit$M5))` of the
  explained variance, and nothing detectable out of sample. Almost all of their
  potential contribution *is* redundant for this outcome. But they are not
  *duplicates* of the categoricals: only
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * summary(lm(danceability ~ genre + artistName, ca))$r.squared)`
  of danceability, `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * summary(lm(energy ~ genre + artistName, ca))$r.squared)`
  of energy and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * summary(lm(tempo ~ genre + artistName, ca))$r.squared)`
  of tempo are explained by genre and artist, so most of their variance is
  information the categoricals genuinely do not carry. They are orthogonal to the
  categoricals **and** uninformative about listening, which is a different thing
  from being redundant, and it recommends something different: keep the features,
  stop expecting them to carry a regression.
* *"The model does not predict playback time out of sample."* **True only on the
  untransformed scale**, and for a reason that is a property of the response rather
  than of the model: the identical specification averages
  `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(raw_r2))` on `msPlayed` in milliseconds (negative in
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(raw_r2 < 0))` of 200 splits) and
  `r sprintf("%.3f", mean(mtx[, "M5"]))` on the log scale. Both numbers are in
  Section 5.1.

**What would still change the answer.** These are the limitations that matter, in
rough order of how much they constrain the reading.

* **Only 3 of the 13 audio variables are modelled.** Key, loudness, mode,
  speechiness, acousticness, instrumentalness, liveness, valence, `duration_ms` and
  `time_signature` never enter. They were inherited from the first version's feature
  selection and not re-derived here, so "the audio attributes are weakly related to
  listening" is a statement about these three, not about the audio block in general.
* **`duration_ms` is the denominator of the skip definition and is never a
  covariate.** Long tracks need more accumulated time to reach one full play, so
  part of what the skip margin measures is track length.
* **The duration-margin estimate conditions on `skip == 0`** — on an outcome of the
  variable being interpreted. It is a conditional association among played tracks,
  not a causal duration effect, and a proper hurdle model would be needed before it
  could be read as one.
* **No multiplicity control.** Roughly a dozen specifications were tested and the
  headline is p = `r sprintf("%.3f", bt$p[4])`; a Bonferroni correction across the
  twelve specifications would put it at roughly 0.05 — marginal by any reading,
  which is the right way to treat it.
* **275 tracks (5.5%) have no audio features** and are excluded on evidence that
  they differ systematically (Section 5.4). The genre taxonomy still puts
  `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(as.character(ca$genre) == "Other"))` of the
  modelling sample in `Other`, which limits what genre can control for.
* **Audio features are algorithmic outputs, not measurements**, so these are not
  clean structural effects and the direction of any bias is unknown.
* **The response is an aggregate over an unobserved listening history** with no
  session, device, timestamp or user information, so omitted context cannot be
  ruled out, and a "skip" here is only an arithmetic fact (`msPlayed < duration`),
  not evidence that anyone decided anything.

# 8. Reproducing this

```{r session}
cat("R", as.character(getRversion()), "|", R.version$platform, "\n")
cat("packages used: stats, graphics",
    if (have_nlme) "+ nlme", "(nlme optional; the analysis runs without it)\n")
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# from the repository root:
rmarkdown::render("Enhanced-Spotify-Attribute-Analysis.rmd")
```

The first version of this analysis, which produced the superseded conclusions, is
preserved unmodified in `../work/v1/` for comparison.
